text.p: Workers are putting the final touches on the massive Ram-Powell deepwater production platform, which is set to be moved next week into the Gulf of Mexico from a fabrication yard here, Shell Oil Co officials said on Tuesday.

Shell's newest tension-leg platform is on track to begin production in August and is expected to be producing at its capacity of 60,000 barrels per day of crude oil by early next year, Shell officials said.

"We should be up to the full capacity on the oil side by the first quarter of 1998," Lisa Johnson, Ram-Powell asset manager, said. The platform also was designed to handle production of about 200 million cubic feet of natural gas per day, she said.

The Ram-Powell platform will produce oil and gas in 3,218 feet of water, breaking a Gulf of Mexico record set by its sister Mars platform installed in 1996 in 2,940 feet of water. But Ram-Powell will be eclipsed in 1999 by Ursa, another Shell tension-leg platform planned for a Mississippi Canyon block in nearly 4,000 feet of water.

The towering 46-story Ram-Powell platform is scheduled to leave the Aker-Gulf Marine Yard here on April 24 and begin an eight-day journey to the Viosca Knoll area of the Gulf, about 80 miles south of Mobile, Ala.
Once in place, a drilling rig perched atop the platform will be used to complete four wells pre-drilled to 5,000 feet.
A total of ten wells are currently planned, including seven producing wells and three water injection wells for sustaining pressure and flow rates from the field.
Shell is the operator of Ram-Powell and controls a 38 percent stake in the $1 billion project, with partners Exxon and Amoco Corp each holding 31 percent stakes, the Shell executives said.

Cloned from Shell's existing Mars production platform, Ram-Powell will produce from reservoirs with estimated gross recovery of 250 million barrels of oil equivalent consisting of half oil and half natural gas.

Shell has been leading the charge into the deepwater Gulf of Mexico, holding stakes in 446 of the 2,095 tracts leased and drilling a third of the exploration and half of the deepwater development wells to date, said Lou Wilkerson, Ram-Powell project manager.
Shell is a unit of Royal Dutch/Shell Group, and its deepwater Gulf of Mexico projects are developed by New Orleans- based Shell Deepwater Development Inc.
